entries.name: Pedunculate oak
entries.fruit: acorns in cups on long stalks
entries.voxel_shape: massive short trunk, broad spreading crown, deeply furrowed bark
entries.notes: The anchor of the European mixed forest: sacred associations, thousands of insect species, acorns feed everything from jays to pigs.

entries.name: European beech
entries.fruit: beechnuts in prickly husks (mast years)
entries.voxel_shape: tall straight grey smooth trunk, dense domed crown
entries.notes: Forms deep shade that few plants tolerate under it; its mast feeds dormice, nuthatches and wild boar.

entries.name: Norway spruce
entries.fruit: long hanging cones 9-17 cm
entries.voxel_shape: huge narrow conical evergreen, spire-like tip
entries.notes: The classic Christmas-tree silhouette; shallow-rooted, so exposed spruce falls in windthrow.

entries.name: Scots pine
entries.fruit: small woody cones, 3-7 cm
entries.voxel_shape: tall straight trunk, bare orange bark above, flat-topped crown
entries.notes: The orange upper bark is unmistakable; oldest pines reach 600-700 years on rocky Scottish crags.

entries.name: Silver birch
entries.fruit: tiny winged nutlets in catkin cylinders
entries.voxel_shape: slender white-peeled trunk, light airy crown of drooping twigs
entries.notes: Pioneer tree: first to colonise burnt or bare ground, pale bark glows in dim woodland.

entries.name: Sweet chestnut
entries.leaves: deciduous, long lanceolate with coarse teeth
entries.flowers: erect catkins, insect pollinated, strong scent
entries.fruit: spiky burrs holding 1-3 glossy brown nuts
entries.voxel_shape: broad trunk often fluted in old trees, wide spreading crown
entries.notes: Ancient coppices in southern Europe are still harvested on 20-30 year rotations; old trunks hollow with age.

entries.name: Common ash
entries.flowers: insignificant tufts before leaves, wind pollinated
entries.fruit: clusters of winged keys (samaras)
entries.voxel_shape: tall trunk with high, open, domed crown and black buds
entries.notes: Prized for tough, springy timber; being devastated across Europe by ash dieback (Hymenoscyphus fraxineus).

entries.name: Norway maple
entries.leaves: deciduous, five-lobed, milky sap in stems
entries.flowers: yellow-green sprays before leaves in April
entries.fruit: paired samaras in wide-angled keys
entries.voxel_shape: rounded dense crown on a short straight trunk
entries.notes: Leaves turn yellow then copper in autumn; sap is milky where sycamore's is clear.

entries.name: Sugar maple
entries.fruit: horseshoe-paired samaras
entries.voxel_shape: tall oval to rounded crown, sturdy columnar trunk
entries.notes: The source of maple syrup; its scarlet-orange autumn spectacle draws crowds across New England and southern Canada.

entries.name: Common hornbeam
entries.leaves: deciduous, doubly serrated with parallel veins
entries.fruit: small ribbed nutlets hanging under three-lobed leafy bracts
entries.voxel_shape: fluted muscular grey trunk, ovoid dense crown
entries.notes: Wood so dense it sinks in water; the traditional choice for mill gears and mallet heads.

entries.name: Small-leaved lime
entries.leaves: deciduous, heart-shaped with tufts of rust hairs beneath
entries.flowers: fragrant yellow-white clusters hanging under a pale bract, July
entries.fruit: small round nutlets in bract-backed clusters
entries.voxel_shape: domed crown, straight trunk, often coppiced into multi-stem stools
entries.notes: The July flowering feeds enormous bee migrations; church and boundary limes are among the longest-lived trees in Europe.

entries.name: European larch
entries.leaves: deciduous conifer, soft needles in rosettes, golden in autumn
entries.fruit: small upright woody cones 2-6 cm
entries.voxel_shape: tall conical conifer with branch-tip tufts of needles
entries.notes: The only common European conifer that drops its needles; turns brilliant gold before falling in autumn.

entries.name: European aspen
entries.leaves: deciduous, near-circular on long flattened stalks (they tremble)
entries.fruit: capsules releasing cottony seeds
entries.voxel_shape: tall straight grey-green column, light fluttering round-leaf crown
entries.notes: Leaves tremble in the slightest breeze; spreads underground into clonal thickets that can cover hillsides.

entries.name: Wild cherry
entries.leaves: deciduous, oval with serrated edges and red stem glands
entries.fruit: red to black cherries, July-August
entries.voxel_shape: straight trunk, cherry-red peeling bark bands, oval crown
entries.notes: Scaly bronze-red bark peels in rings; its timber is the classic cabinet-maker's cherry.

entries.name: Rowan
entries.fruit: bright orange-red pomes (mountain ash berries)
entries.voxel_shape: small slender tree, grey bark, flat-topped crown with berry clusters
entries.notes: Grows to the tree line and above; folklore holds it protects against enchantment and ill luck.

entries.name: European holly
entries.fruit: scarlet drupes on female trees only (winter)
entries.voxel_shape: dense cone of glossy dark foliage on a short pale trunk
entries.notes: Only female plants carry the red berries; holly timber is one of the few pale native carving woods.

entries.name: European yew
entries.leaves: evergreen, flat dark needles in two ranks
entries.fruit: fleshy red arils around a single poisonous seed
entries.voxel_shape: massive dark dome, often hollow and twisted in antiquity
entries.notes: Among the longest-lived organisms on Earth; nearly all parts are fatally poisonous, only the aril flesh is sweet.

entries.name: Eastern white pine
entries.leaves: evergreen, soft needles in bundles of five
entries.fruit: long slender cones 8-20 cm with resin
entries.voxel_shape: towering soft column with a feathery crown and bare lower trunk
entries.notes: Colonial-era boards and masts of this species built fleets; designated 'King's Broad Arrow' trees were reserved for the Royal Navy.

entries.name: Common hazel
entries.flowers: yellow male catkins ('lamb's tails') with tiny red female tufts, February-March
entries.fruit: hazelnuts in frilled green husks
entries.voxel_shape: multi-stemmed rounded bush, often in cut stools
entries.notes: The key coppice understory; nuts feed dormice, nuthatches, jays and people, and the wood spars into perfect fence rods.

entries.name: Elder
entries.flowers: flat creamy umbels in June, strong elderflower scent
entries.fruit: dense black-purple berry bunches, August-September
entries.voxel_shape: straggly multi-stemmed bush, corky fissured bark, flat flower plates
uses: blowguns and whistles from hollow pithy stems
entries.notes: Hollow corky stems were drilled out into whistles and blowguns; birds are the main seed dispersers, so elder springs up near old fields.

entries.name: Common hawthorn
entries.flowers: white mayflower clusters in May, smell of trimethylamine (midge-pollinated)
entries.fruit: red haws, autumn
entries.voxel_shape: knotted thorny dome, dense hedge-like mass
entries.notes: The 'may tree'; its scent of decay attracts pollinating flies. Lone thorn bushes are fairy sites in British folklore — never cut one.

entries.name: Blackthorn
entries.flowers: white on bare thorny twigs in March
entries.fruit: black sloes, eye-wateringly astringent
entries.voxel_shape: black-barked thorny tangle, near-impenetrable
entries.notes: Flowers on bare black twigs before any leaves, then swallows whole fields via root suckers; the classic impenetrable hedge.

entries.name: Bramble
entries.growth: very fast (arching canes root where they touch)
entries.fruit: black blackberries, August-September
entries.voxel_shape: arching thorny cane thickets scrambling over ground and banks
entries.notes: Not one species but hundreds of microspecies; a wall of bramble is prime songbird nesting cover and free late-summer fruit.

entries.name: Common ivy
entries.leaves: evergreen, lobed dark leaves (unlobed on flowering shoots)
entries.flowers: green globes in October — the last major nectar source of the year
entries.fruit: black berries ripening in late winter (birds only; toxic to mammals)
entries.fire: killed (previously prized as a hot-burning fuel)
entries.voxel_shape: evergreen carpet climbing tree trunks and walls in sheets
entries.notes: Flowers when almost nothing else does; ivy on a tree supports more species than any other British plant. Mostly harmless to healthy trees.

entries.name: Common bracken
entries.leaves: deciduous triangular fronds, dead-orange in autumn
entries.fruit: spores under rolled frond edges (rarely fertile)
entries.voxel_shape: tall sturdy triangular fronds on single stalks, arching
entries.notes: Carcinogenic (ptaquiloside) — not safe as fodder or eaten raw; spreads relentlessly by rhizome and is a notorious pasture invader.

entries.name: Male fern
entries.fruit: spores in round sori under the fronds
entries.voxel_shape: rosette of arching divided fronds from a scaly crown
entries.notes: The archetypal woodland fern; its scaly rhizome crown is dense with old frond bases, like a small pineapple.

entries.name: Red-stemmed feather moss
entries.leaves: evergreen scale-like leaves on reddish stems
entries.fruit: spores in capsules on setae
entries.fire: killed above ground; regrows from base
entries.voxel_shape: soft feathery carpet with red stems
entries.notes: Carpet-forming moss of conifer and mixed forest floors; a key peat-former and nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria host.

entries.name: Oakmoss
entries.fruit: spores in tiny discs on the thallus
entries.voxel_shape: grey-green forked fruticose cushions clinging to bark
entries.notes: The fixative behind classic chypre perfumes; its presence signals unpolluted air — it vanishes from cities under sulphur dioxide.

entries.name: Wood anemone
entries.flowers: white (sometimes pink/purple-backed) star-like, April, no true petals
entries.fruit: small woolly nutlets
entries.voxel_shape: low white star flowers above a single whorl of leaves
entries.notes: Paints the woodland floor white for three weeks before the canopy closes; an indicator of ancient, undisturbed woodland.

entries.name: Common bluebell
entries.flowers: nodding violet-blue one-sided racemes in May, sweet scent
entries.fruit: three-lobed capsule of black seeds
entries.voxel_shape: drooping wands of violet bells leaning one way
entries.notes: Britain holds about half the world's bluebells; the bulb starch ('sap') once stiffened bookbinders' glues and sleeve ruffs.

entries.name: Ramsons (wild garlic)
entries.fruit: three-angled capsule of black seeds
entries.voxel_shape: broad low garlic-scented leaves wall-to-wall, white pompom flowers
entries.notes: Carpets damp shady woodland with garlic scent; bears dig the bulbs after hibernation — hence ursinum.

entries.name: Foxglove
entries.flowers: tall one-sided spikes of purple-pink spotted bells June-July
entries.fruit: capsule releasing thousands of dust-like seeds
entries.fire: killed (germinates well on bare ground after fire)
entries.voxel_shape: tall single spike of hanging bells above a rosette
entries.notes: Every part is potentially lethal — source of the heart drug digoxin, standardised from it in 1785. Spotted throat marks guide bees.

entries.name: Wood sorrel
entries.leaves: deciduous, three heart-shaped leaflets like a clover
entries.flowers: white with lilac veins, May-June; petals fold shut at night and in rain
entries.fruit: small capsule that explosively ejects its seeds
entries.voxel_shape: tiny shamrock-like triple-leaf clumps
uses: edible sour leaves (oxalic acid; small amounts)
entries.notes: Not a clover — the sour snap is oxalic acid. Favoured of shade gardeners and foragers; ancient-woodland indicator again.

entries.name: Enchanter's nightshade
entries.leaves: deciduous ovals opposite on an upright stem
entries.fruit: two-chambered burs covered in hooked bristles (animal-dispersed)
entries.voxel_shape: low upright stems with small pink flower wands
uses: historical topical herb (name from circe, the enchantress)
entries.notes: The velcro-burr of the woodland — an ancestor of burdock-like hooked dispersal. Its specialised flea beetle (Altica circaeae) eats little else.

entries.name: Wild strawberry
entries.flowers: white five-petalled in small clusters, April-June
entries.fruit: small fragrant red false berries (achenes on the receptacle), June-July
entries.voxel_shape: low triple-leaf clumps speckled with tiny white flowers then tiny fruit
entries.notes: Intensely flavoured — the benchmark against which cultivated strawberries are measured; spreads by runners along woodland edges.

entries.name: Wood meadow-grass
entries.flowers: loose panicle of small spikelets, June-August
entries.fruit: one-seeded caryopses in spikelets
entries.voxel_shape: delicate loose tufted grass with an open nodding panicle
entries.notes: One of the few grasses at home in deep woodland shade; common along rides and glades.

entries.name: Fly agaric
entries.fruit: white gills shedding spores from under a red, white-spotted cap
entries.fire: fruit bodies killed; mycelium survives in soil
entries.voxel_shape: toadstool: red cap with white warts on a white stalk with a skirt
entries.notes: The fairy-tale toadstool; forms mycorrhizal partnerships with birch and pine, so look under those trees in September. Sacred in Siberian shamanism.

entries.name: Porcini (cep)
entries.fruit: olive-brown tubes (pores) under a bun-brown cap
entries.fire: fruit bodies killed; mycelium survives in soil
entries.voxel_shape: thick-stalked brown dome, white netting on the swollen stem
entries.notes: The gold standard wild mushroom; strictly mycorrhizal, so it cannot be farmed — a good porcini spot is guarded like a secret.

entries.name: Chanterelle
entries.fruit: blunt gill-like folds (false gills), egg-yolk orange, faint apricot scent
entries.fire: fruit bodies killed; mycelium survives in soil
entries.voxel_shape: solid trumpet of egg-yolk orange funnels
entries.notes: Apricot-scented egg-yolk trumpet; fakes are rare but check the folds — true chanterelles have smooth forked ridges, never blade-like gills.

entries.name: Honey fungus
entries.growth: seasonal clusters on dead wood (mycelium can spread for centuries)
entries.fruit: dense clusters of honey-brown caps with white ring, on stumps and roots; black rhizomorph 'bootlaces' under bark
entries.voxel_shape: tight honey-coloured clusters sprouting from stumps, black cords beneath bark
entries.notes: The largest known organisms on Earth are honey-fungus clones (one Oregon clone covers ~900 ha and may be ~2400 years old); it kills weakened trees from the roots.
